8[(a) be a person possessing highest level of competence, integrity, morals and institutional commitment;

(e) is a member of, or be otherwise associated with, any political party or any organisation which takes part in politics, or is taking part in or subscribing in aid of, any political movement or activity;
Explanation.- For purposes of this sub-clause, whether any party is a political party, or whether any organisation takes part in politics or whether any movement or activity falls within the scope of this sub-clause, the decision of the Kuladhipati thereon shall be final:

Summary of Delhi Land Holdings (Ceiling) Act, 1960
The Delhi Land Holdings (Ceiling) Act, 1960 was enacted to impose a ceiling on the ownership of agricultural land in the Union Territory of Delhi. The Act sought to prevent the concentration of land in the hands of a few individuals, promote equitable distribution of agricultural land, and implement land reforms. It provided for the acquisition of surplus land by the Government and its redistribution to eligible landless persons and small farmers, while recognizing certain exemptions.
Objective
The main objectives of the Act are:
•	To impose a ceiling on agricultural land holdings in Delhi.
•	To prevent concentration of land ownership and eliminate large landholdings.
•	To acquire surplus agricultural land for public purposes.
•	To promote equitable distribution of land among landless persons and small farmers.
•	To implement land reforms and encourage social and economic justice in rural areas.
Key Provisions
1.	Ceiling on Land Holdings
o	The Act prescribed the maximum extent of agricultural land that an individual or family could legally own or hold.
2.	Declaration of Land Holdings
o	Landholders were required to furnish declarations regarding the extent and nature of their agricultural land holdings to the prescribed authority.
3.	Determination of Surplus Land
o	The competent authority determined the land held in excess of the prescribed ceiling limit after verification of declarations and relevant records.
4.	Acquisition of Surplus Land
o	Land declared surplus vested in the Government, free from encumbrances, in accordance with the provisions of the Act.
5.	Redistribution of Land
o	Surplus land acquired by the Government could be allotted to landless agricultural labourers, small farmers, and other eligible beneficiaries as prescribed.
6.	Exemptions
o	The Act provided exemptions for specified categories of land or institutions, subject to the conditions laid down under the Act.
7.	Compensation
o	It contained provisions regarding the payment of compensation to persons whose surplus land was acquired by the Government.
8.	Appeals and Revision
o	Persons aggrieved by orders of the competent authority could file appeals or seek revision before the prescribed appellate authority.
9.	Penalties
o	The Act prescribed penalties for furnishing false information, concealing land holdings, or violating its provisions.
10.	Rule-Making Power
•	The Central Government was empowered to make rules for carrying out the purposes of the Act.

If an arrear of public Revenue shall accrue on an estate ordered to be divided, while the partition of the estate is being made, any one or more of the proprietors may tender to the Collector his or their quota of the balance, and the Collector shall receive the same, and credit the amount to the share or shares of such proprietor or proprietors.
If a sale of any part of the estate shall ultimately become necessary for the liquidation of any part of such arrear which may remain due, only the share or shares of the proprietor or proprietors who shall not have contributed their quota of the balance shall be sold in the first instance, and the partition shall go on and be completed, in the same manner as if no arrear of public Revenue had accrued.
The purchaser or purchasers of the share or shares sold shall be entitled to separate possession of the estate or estates which, under the partition, would have been allotted to the defaulting proprietor or proprietors.
Provided always that, in all cases of a partition, the entire estate shall be considered responsible for the public Revenue assessed upon it, until the partition shall have been completed, and the several proprietors shall have been put into possession of the separate estates into which the estate may be ordered to be divided, according as the same may be allotted to them.

Summary of The National Dental Commission Act, 2023 
I. Overview
•	Title & Scope: Regulates the dentistry profession across India, ensuring quality education and healthcare, with specific provisions for temporary registrations for practitioners from other states or countries under certain conditions.
•	Commencement: Effective from specified dates, including February 29, 2024, for key sections.
•	Objective: To enhance the quality of dental education, make it affordable, and improve accessibility to high-quality oral healthcare, considering the integration of existing state-level practices.
II. Key Components
•	National Dental Commission (NDC):
•	Role: Overseeing dentistry regulation in India, harmonizing state and national standards.
•	Autonomous Boards:
1.	Dental Assessment and Rating Board: Evaluates dental institutions, considering state-specific accreditation.
2.	Ethics and Dental Registration Board: Manages ethical standards and registrations, including temporary ones for out-of-state practitioners.
3.	Under-Graduate and Post-Graduate Dental Education Board: Regulates dental education, aligning with the Medical Practitioners Act's principles.
•	Dental Advisory Council: Provides policy and regulatory advice, incorporating feedback from state dental councils.
III. Regulatory Framework
•	Qualification Recognition:
•	Domestic & Interstate: Managed by the Under-Graduate and Post-Graduate Dental Education Board, with provisions for state-qualified practitioners.
•	Foreign: Requires passing the National Exit Test (Dental) or Screening Test, with temporary registration options under specific conditions (e.g., principal livelihood for at least two years).
•	Registration Process:
•	National & State Registers: For dentists and dental auxiliaries, with clear pathways for temporary to permanent registration based on practice duration and location.
•	Temporary Registration: Detailed conditions for out-of-state or foreign citizens, including a five-year temporary registration for those practicing as principal livelihood for at least two years prior to application.
IV. Education and Assessments
•	Entrance and Exit Tests:
•	National Eligibility-cum-Entrance Test (Dental): For undergraduate admissions, applicable nationwide.
•	National Exit Test (Dental): For graduation, licensing, and validation of foreign and interstate qualifications.
V. Governance and Oversight
•	Central Government Oversight:
•	Directional Powers: Over NDC and Autonomous Boards, ensuring uniform application across states.
•	Provision for Supersession: Of the NDC under extraordinary circumstances, protecting the integrity of the profession.
•	Legal Protections: For actions taken in good faith, including those related to temporary registrations and interstate practice approvals.
VI. Financial Provisions and Audits
•	Funding Source: Central Government grants, potentially supplemented by state contributions for specific initiatives.
•	Audit Authority: Comptroller and Auditor General of India, ensuring transparency across all financial transactions.

The National Dental Commission Act, 2023 

Source: Official Record of Parliament, India Code, and Ministry of Health and Family Welfare

Act Title - The National Dental Commission Act, 2023
Act Number - Act No. 21 of 2023 
Act ID (India Code) - 202321
 Presidential Assent date - August 11, 2023 
 Enforcement Date - February 29,2024
Nodal Ministry - Ministry of Health and Family Welfare 

Precedent & Historical Rationale
●	Repeal and Overhaul of Legacy Regulatory Framework: Repeals the Dentists Act, 1948 (16 of 1948) and dissolves the Dental Council of India (DCI) to modernize dental education, practice, and ethics across the country.
●	Establishment of the National Dental Commission (NDC): Sets up the National Dental Commission alongside three autonomous boards—the Under-Graduate and Post-Graduate Dental Education Board, the Dental Education Assessment and Rating Board, and the Ethics and Dental Registration Board—mirroring the regulatory structure of the National Medical Commission (NMC).
●	Standardized Qualifications and Exit Exams: Mandates the National Exit Test (Dental) [NEXT-D] for licensing and postgraduate admissions, standardizes uniform registration across State Registers, and regulates fee structures for a specified percentage of seats in private dental institutions.
 
Parliamentary Trajectory & Enactment
●	Formulation: Introduced by the Union Minister of Health and Family Welfare, Dr. Mansukh Mandaviya, to overhaul the governance of dental education, make high-quality oral healthcare accessible, and eliminate regulatory opacity.
●	Parliamentary Passage: Introduced in the Lok Sabha on July 24, 2023; passed by the Lok Sabha on July 28, 2023; and passed by the Rajya Sabha on August 8, 2023.
●	Presidential Assent: Received the assent of the President of India on August 11, 2023.
●	Enforcement: Enforced on February 29,2024.
